title: Bhrigu's five answers
hookLine: a son asks his father to teach him the ultimate, and is sent back to look again, and again
carry: five sheaths, and the one who sees them
last: DON'T BE AFRAID. THERE IS A WAY.

cards: A young man named Bhrigu goes to his father, Varuna, and says: sir, teach me Brahman. The ultimate. Just tell me.
His father doesn't lecture. He says, roughly: it's that from which all beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return. Seek it through tapas, deep, disciplined searching.
So Bhrigu goes off, searches hard, and comes back with an answer. His father doesn't say right or wrong. Go back, he says.

teach.b: This is the Taittiriya Upanishad, and Bhrigu searches five times. First he decides Brahman is food: everything is born from food, lives on food, goes back to the earth. Then breath, the life force.
Then mind, the stream of thoughts and wants. Then understanding, the part that decides and says, I'm doing this. Each time, his father sends him deeper.
At last Bhrigu sees: bliss, ananda, is Brahman.

Earlier in the same Upanishad, those five appear as layers of a person, one inside another, and later Vedanta teachers call them koshas, sheaths: food, breath, mind, understanding, bliss. Here's the Advaita reading.

Each sheath is something you can notice: the body, the breath, thoughts coming and going, yourself deciding. Even the peace of dreamless sleep, you notice arriving and leaving. So none of them is the one noticing.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO NOTICES ALL FIVE.
teach.b: The self, Shankara's school says, shines through all five, the way the sun shines through colored glass without becoming colored. An honest note: Hindu schools read this differently.
Shankara's school says even the bliss sheath is still a covering. Others, including Ramanuja's, read the passage's bliss as pointing to Brahman itself.
Same text, two readings. And today? The five koshas turn up in yoga classes everywhere now, and they come from here.
But the teaching is bigger than a stretch. On a day when you feel you are your tired body, or your racing thoughts, or one bad decision, Advaita says: those are layers you can see.
You're the one seeing them. Bhrigu didn't stop at the first answer, and you don't have to either.

how: Many Vedanta and yoga teachers use the five koshas from the Taittiriya Upanishad as a map for contemplation, moving attention inward from the body through breath, mind and understanding to bliss, as Bhrigu did, and in Advaita to the witness beyond them.

o: a story about a son who never found an answer
a belief that the body is all you really are
the self as awareness, not apart from Brahman

games.q: Bhrigu's five answers — tap the pairs.
p: sent back to search again and again

s: the five koshas are a modern yoga-studio idea
they come from the Taittiriya Upanishad, the same text that tells of Bhrigu.
Bhrigu's father kept sending him back to search again
each time, Varuna told him to seek Brahman through tapas, until he reached bliss.
in Shankara's school, the bliss sheath is the self
even the bliss sheath is a covering; the self is the awareness shining through all five.

games.q: you notice your body, your breath, your thoughts, your decisions, even a moment of bliss. in Shankara's school, which one are you?
o: none: you're what notices all five.
the mind: it's doing the noticing.
games.why: each sheath can be noticed, so none is the noticer. the self shines through them, like sun through colored glass.

practice: Go inward the way Bhrigu did, one layer at a time: the body's weight and warmth, the breath going in and out, a thought or a plan or a worry, then the part that wonders, am I doing this right?
If a little peace shows up, notice that too. Then rest as the one who noticed all five, for as long as it lasts.

wordCard.voice: Advaita, through the five sheaths Bhrigu passed through: food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss. In Shankara's school, the self is the awareness shining through all five.

orig.note: Sanskrit: pancha (five) + kosha (sheath, covering, treasury): the five sheaths.

carryVoice: Your line: five sheaths, and the one who sees them. Bhrigu kept going deeper. That's two eighty-six.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1–5 (the five selves or sheaths)
Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1–6 (Bhrigu seeks Brahman from his father Varuna: food, breath, mind, understanding, bliss)
Brahma Sutra 1.1.12–19 and the commentaries of Shankara and Ramanuja (the anandamaya)
